1.why: The /api/verify handler rejects any code whose reset record accountKey does not match the session's recoveryAccountKey, and password grants are additionally bound to sessionId and accountKey.

2.why: Codes are SHA-256-hashed, single-use (reset.used set immediately on verification), and tied to the requesting session's account, so a code issued for one user cannot be replayed for another.

3.why: Only the resetting session's authority is cleared via clearAccountAuthority(); sessions are stored independently with no per-account revocation, so any other pre-existing authenticated session would remain valid after a reset.

4.why: HTTPS is mandatory (non-HTTPS requests are rejected, HSTS is set, TLS certs are loaded), but no explicit minimum/latest TLS version is configured, so 'latest TLS version' cannot be confirmed.

5.why: Reset codes are stored as SHA-256 hashes, passwords are hashed with bcrypt, and approved identifiers are stored hashed — appropriate protection, though this is hashing rather than encryption as literally worded.

6.why: There is no real email; the simulated delivery is guarded by session state and carries no patient data, but the working recovery code is intentionally returned to the browser and written into the demo activity log.

7.why: Identifiers and tokens are validated with strict regexes, passwords go through a policy check, JSON parsing is guarded, and all client-side rendering uses textContent/DOM nodes rather than HTML injection.

8.why: The only redirect target is the fixed, server-generated relative path /recovery-link?token=..., with no external or user-controlled redirect anywhere in the code.

9.why: No email templates exist; the simulated delivery is plain JSON and no user input is ever rendered as HTML (textContent plus a strict nonce-based CSP), so the claim holds vacuously.

10.why: Error responses are generic with no stack traces, but the real, usable recovery code and the MFA code are deliberately written to the browser console and the on-page activity logs.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and reset tokens are stored hashed, but the MFA code '246810' and a default account password hash are hardcoded directly in the source.

12.why: The shipped default password hash is the well-known public bcrypt example hash (of 'password') and the MFA code is a fixed constant, so default credentials effectively work unless overridden via environment variables.

13.why: Every sensitive endpoint (login, recovery, verify, password, MFA) is throttled per-session and per-source+account with 429 responses and retry-after messaging after 5–8 attempts per 15 minutes.

14.why: Recovery and login return identical generic messages whether or not the account exists; only a minor timing difference (bcrypt verify skipped for unknown accounts) and the intentional on-page display of the synthetic demo identifier weaken this.

15.why: Reset codes are 256-bit cryptographically random tokens, stored as SHA-256 hashes, single-use, expiring after 15 minutes, and bound to the specific account and session.
